copy.programOverviewCopy: Core Basics lays the foundation for addressing common peri through postmenopausal challenges like diastasis recti, pelvic organ prolapse, leaking, painful intimacy, back pain, and even anxiety and bowel issues. This program teaches you how to reconnect with your core and pelvic floor in a way that supports strength, function, and confidence.

intro.introVideoCopy:
Let’s get one thing straight right out of the gate: this work...it’s not flashy. It can feel boring, humbling, and straight-up frustrating. But it is so important. In fact, I’d argue it might be the most important thing you EVER learn about your body.

Most of us have spent decades sucking in our belly because society told you to be smaller. That constant “hold it in” habit leads to dysfunctional breathing and a core that doesn’t know how to truly engage. As a result, we experience leaks, prolapse and discomfort with penetration.

Take the time to work through the lessons and each Core Basics level. You'll be so glad you did.

introLessons.lessonCopy: Pelvic organ prolapse (POP) is when one or more of the pelvic organs—like the bladder, uterus, or rectum—drop from their usual position and press into the vaginal wall. In perimenopause, this often happens because declining estrogen levels lead to weaker, thinner muscles and tissues that normally offer support. It’s not dangerous, but it can be uncomfortable. The good news? Many cases can be managed without surgery, and support is out there—you’re not alone in this.

Your "six-pack" muscles may get all the attention, but your core is a full team effort—layers of muscles working together to support your spine, organs, and everyday movement. Diastasis recti happens when the connective tissue between your abdominal muscles (the linea alba) stretches and thins, leaving a gap down the midline. It’s not usually painful, but it can lead to core weakness, back discomfort, pelvic floor issues, and yep—that stubborn belly bulge that doesn’t seem to budge. The good news? It’s common and it’s treatable! With the right strategies and support, you can rebuild strength and feel more at home in your body.

Your breath should match the effort of what you're doing. Think of it like volume control. Picking up a 25-pound bag of dog food? That calls for a solid inhale, then a strong, audible exhale as you lift. Just grabbing a jug of milk? A smaller exhale and light brace will do the job. The goal is to exhale on the effort—that’s the hard part of the movement.

So when I cue you to “audibly exhale”—I mean it! Give me a big HAAAA or SSSSS. That sound helps fully engage your core and pelvic floor, and gives your diaphragm room to move. It might feel weird at first, but trust me—this kind of weird is working for you.

For example, in a deadlift: inhale as you hinge down, then exhale with intention as you stand tall. (Bonus points if your dog looks confused by your sound effects.)

And just a heads-up: this advice is for lifts under 80% of your one-rep max. If you're lifting super heavy—like max-effort stuff—you might need a different breath strategy. But if you're still healing your core or pelvic floor, max lifting can wait. First, let’s build a strong, symptom-free foundation.

Breath is strength. Make it work with you—not against you.

intro.beforeYouBeginCopy: If possible, I highly recommend seeing a pelvic floor physical therapist for a hands-on assessment. Even just one or two sessions can provide valuable insight into how your body is functioning and guide you toward the best path for strength and healing.
